subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 4 periods = 160 minutes
Total: 4 periods · 2h 40min

periods.activity_title: Reading the Neem Baba Dialogue Aloud

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.80): How is neem useful to farmers?
Let us discuss (p.80): Mention some uses of the neem tree.

homework.task_brief: Let us read (p.78): Complete the neem fact sheet — names, origins, scientists' labels.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the dialogue aloud — Parts I and II — with students following in their textbooks (pp.75–80). Pause briefly after each exchange to let students absorb Neem Baba's revelations about origins, names, and medicinal properties.

Open a brief whole-class discussion on “Let us discuss” (p.80): How does neem help farmers? Students draw on the dialogue passages about locusts, mosquito breeding, crop yield, and termite protection.
Students pair up to answer “Mention some uses of the neem tree” (p.80), listing uses across agriculture, medicine, household, and industry. Two or three pairs share answers aloud.
Teacher sets the fact-sheet homework from “Let us read” (p.78) — students will complete it independently using the text they have just heard.

periods.teacher_notes: The dialogue is rich with technical detail — neem’s Sanskrit names and chemical properties can feel dense on a first encounter, so a warm, expressive read-aloud helps students absorb meaning before written tasks. Students often conflate medicinal and agricultural uses; press them to name the specific part of the neem tree involved in each use. Tasks on neem’s origins and scientists’ epithets (p.78) are not covered in class; students interested in those details may revisit that section independently.

periods.activity_title: Comprehension Reflection and Listening to Peepal Baba

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.81): Complete four sentences on neem’s properties and uses.
Let us think and reflect (p.81): Which parts of the neem tree are used medicinally?
Let us listen (p.83): Select the correct statements about Peepal Baba.

time_bands.activity: Students complete the four sentence-completion items from “Let us think and reflect” (p.81) individually, drawing on the dialogue. Teacher circulates and prompts students who hesitate — for example, recalling Amber’s question about measles and Neem Baba’s reply about neem leaves destroying germs.
Whole-class discussion: “Which parts of the neem tree are used in medicine?” (p.81). Students list leaves, bark, flowers, fruits, and roots, and teacher notes each part on the board with its use.

Teacher reads the Peepal Baba conversation (p.101) aloud twice at natural pace. Students listen and then mark which statements from “Let us listen” (p.83) are correct, working individually before a quick show-of-hands check.
Teacher briefly clarifies any disputed statement from the listening task, pointing to the specific exchange in the transcript that confirms or disproves it.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who have read about Amber’s dialogue with Neem Baba will recognise that Peepal Baba’s story echoes the same theme of trees as givers of life — this connection helps the listening feel purposeful rather than detached. A common slip is marking the statement about the mother’s attitude as false; draw attention to her final lines about learning from Peepal Baba. Two tasks from “Let us think and reflect” — the thought-provoking reflection and the two surprising facts — are not covered in class; students may explore them as personal writing.

periods.activity_title: Leaf Stories: Speaking and Writing About Trees

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (p.83): Leaf-card presentation — draw, describe, invite classmates to identify.
Let us write (p.84): Write a paragraph about a tree in your neighbourhood.

time_bands.activity: Teacher explains the leaf-card activity: each student quickly sketches a leaf shape on a slip of paper, writes the tree’s name and one use on the reverse, drawing on any leaves they know from their surroundings or from the neem dialogue.

Three or four volunteers hold up their leaf sketch, describe the process of drawing it, and invite classmates to name the tree and state a use before revealing their card. Teacher models confident spoken delivery — clear voice, addressing the class.

Students independently write a paragraph about a tree they know from their neighbourhood (p.84), covering its location, appearance (height, trunk, leaves, flowers), and why they value it. Teacher circulates, prompting specificity — “tell me what the trunk looks like” — and helps students draft a title.
Two students read their paragraph aloud. Class offers one word of response each. Teacher collects finished paragraphs.

periods.teacher_notes: The speaking activity is designed for students who may not have collected dry leaves in advance — a quick sketch on paper serves the same purpose and removes any preparation barrier. In the writing task, students often describe only appearance and omit the personal reason for liking the tree; prompt them to include at least one specific medicinal, ecological, or emotional reason, echoing the kind of detail Neem Baba shared. Students who do not finish their paragraph in class should complete it at home using the same prompts on p.84.

periods.activity_title: Compound Words, Verb Tenses, and Neem’s Many Names

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.81): Sort compound words into open, closed, and hyphenated categories.
Let us learn (p.82): Match present-tense verbs to their past-tense forms.
Let us explore (p.84): Match regional neem names to their Indian languages.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes the nine compound words from “Let us learn” (p.81) on the board and explains the three types — open, closed, hyphenated — with one example each. Students sort all nine words individually, then compare with a neighbour before a whole-class check.

Teacher introduces the present-to-past verb matching table (p.82), reminding students that the neem dialogue uses both tenses as Neem Baba moves between past history and present uses. Students match all six pairs and compose one sentence using any form they choose.

Teacher briefly explains how the name Azadirachta indica came from the Persian phrase “Azad Darakhte Hindi”, then students discuss in pairs which Indian language each of the seven regional neem names — Nimb, Nim, Leemba, Nimori, Nimbamond, Nimbe, Nimo — might belong to, using any knowledge of regional languages in the class.

Students note down the regional names they were unsure about for further inquiry at home or in the library. Teacher closes by connecting the spread of neem’s names to the tree’s own story of spreading across continents.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often place “well known” and “well trained” in the closed category because “well” feels attached; take time to show that the space between the two words is retained in open compounds. The personification task from “Let us learn” is not covered in class — it may be raised as a short class discussion if time permits, or students may note examples from the dialogue independently. For the regional-names task, a class with students from diverse linguistic backgrounds is a rich resource; invite them to share what they recognise.

items.source_lo: Student retrieves and organises factual information from a dialogue using the dialogue text as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Neem tree’s agricultural uses, medicinal parts, and practical benefits described by Neem Baba.
items.item_stem: In the dialogue, Neem Baba explains several ways the neem tree helps farmers. Which of the following is one benefit Neem Baba describes?

options.label: A
options.text: Neem bark is ground into a paste that waterproofs irrigation channels.

options.label: B
options.text: Neem flowers are dried and fed to cattle to increase milk production.

options.label: C
options.text: Neem roots are boiled to create a fertiliser that doubles wheat yield.

options.label: D
options.text: Neem seed powder is sprinkled on crops to deter locusts.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Student may be conflating the general idea of neem benefiting crops with a specific fertiliser use that does not appear in the dialogue.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student may be generalising from neem’s medicinal properties to an animal-feed use that Neem Baba does not mention.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student may be confusing the waterproofing or preservative qualities of neem products with an irrigation application not present in the text.

items.source_lo: Student retrieves and organises factual information from a dialogue using the dialogue text as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Neem tree’s agricultural uses, medicinal parts, and practical benefits described by Neem Baba.
items.item_stem: In the dialogue, Amber already knows some uses of neem before Neem Baba explains more. Based on the dialogue, what does this suggest about the relationship between everyday knowledge and scientific understanding of the neem tree? Support your answer with one detail from the conversation.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Amber’s existing knowledge — such as using neem twigs to clean teeth and placing neem leaves with stored clothes — shows that everyday practice had already recognised the tree’s benefits long before science explained the reasons. Neem Baba then adds the scientific explanation, for example that neem’s chemical properties destroy germs, showing that folk knowledge and science point in the same direction.

items.source_lo: Student identifies accurate information and evaluates statements by listening critically to a spoken conversation.
items.source_context: A boy tells his mother about Peepal Baba — a tree-planting activist who began as a child in Pune.
items.item_stem: Listen to the conversation between Rahul and his mother about Peepal Baba. Read the statements below and decide which are TRUE and which are FALSE.

options.text: Peepal Baba got the idea to plant trees from his English teacher in Pune.
Peepal Baba was born into a family of farmers in Pune.
People initially used the name ‘Peepal Baba’ to make fun of him.
Rahul’s mother thinks no one should bother learning from Peepal Baba’s example.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. True — Rahul says his English teacher in Pune gave him the idea when he was eleven.
2. False — Peepal Baba was born to an army officer’s family in Chandigarh, not a farming family in Pune.
3. True — Rahul says people made fun of him by calling him Peepal Baba, but he continued his work.
4. False — Rahul’s mother says they should learn from him and plant more trees.

items.source_lo: Student identifies accurate information and evaluates statements by listening critically to a spoken conversation.
items.source_context: A boy tells his mother about Peepal Baba — a tree-planting activist who began as a child in Pune.
items.item_stem: In the conversation, Rahul describes how Peepal Baba turned a name that was meant to mock him into a name of respect. What does this tell you about Peepal Baba’s character? Give one reason from the conversation to support your answer.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Peepal Baba’s character shows determination and indifference to ridicule — Rahul says he was not bothered by people mocking him and simply continued planting trees, so the name eventually became a term of affection.

items.item_stem: Amber learns from Neem Baba that every part of the neem tree — leaves, bark, flowers, fruits, and roots — has a use. Imagine that a tree in your neighbourhood could speak, just as Neem Baba spoke to Amber. Write a paragraph in which the tree tells one person what it gives to the world and why it deserves to be protected.

expected_elements: Writes from the tree’s perspective in first person.
Names at least two specific benefits the tree provides.
Includes a plea or reason for protection grounded in those benefits.
Uses descriptive language appropriate to the tree’s voice and character.

items.source_context: Compound words from the dialogue sorted by type; present-tense verbs matched to their past-tense forms.
items.item_stem:
The sentences below are about the neem tree, but each uses the wrong tense of the verb shown in brackets. Rewrite each sentence using the correct past-tense form of the verb, and explain in one sentence why you chose that form.
1. Scientists (discover) many uses of the neem tree over centuries.
2. Neem Baba (tell) Amber about the tree’s ancient origins.
3. Farmers (find) that neem seed powder kept locusts away.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. Scientists discovered many uses of the neem tree over centuries — ‘discovered’ is the simple past of ‘discover’, used because the action was completed in the past. 2. Neem Baba told Amber about the tree’s ancient origins — ‘told’ is the irregular past of ‘tell’. 3. Farmers found that neem seed powder kept locusts away — ‘found’ is the irregular past of ‘find’.

items.item_stem: The dialogue explains that the scientific name of neem, Azadirachta indica, came from the Persian phrase ‘Azad Darakhte Hindi’. Neem also has different names across Indian languages. Research and complete the table below: for each regional name, identify the Indian language it belongs to and the state or region where that language is spoken.
items.visual_stimulus:
Regional name | Indian language | State or region
Nimb | | 
Nim | | 
Leemba | | 
Nimori | | 
Nimbamond | | 
Nimbe | | 
Nimo | |

expected_elements: Identifies the language family for at least four of the seven names.
Connects each name to a recognisable Indian state or region.
Notes that the variety of names reflects the tree’s widespread presence.
Draws a brief conclusion linking linguistic diversity to the tree’s cultural importance.

items.source_lo: Student investigates the linguistic and cultural origins of a subject through interdisciplinary inquiry using the dialogue as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Regional Indian names for neem — Nimb, Nim, Leemba, Nimori, Nimbamond, Nimbe, Nimo — and their language origins.
items.item_stem: Neem Baba tells Amber that when Iranians saw the tree growing freely in India, they called it ‘Azad Darakhte Hindi’ — the free tree of India. Based on your research into the regional names of neem, write a short paragraph explaining what the many different names of the neem tree tell us about the relationship between a plant and the people who live alongside it. Use at least two specific names from your research as examples.

expected_elements: Uses at least two researched regional names as specific examples.
Explains that different names reflect local languages and cultures.
Makes a connection between the tree’s widespread use and its many names.
Presents ideas in a coherent paragraph with a clear concluding thought.
